opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and it gets at something I think is underappreciated in how we design sequence models.

If you look at most attention-style or linear-recurrent architectures through the lens of associative memory, you have keys, values, and a memory that learns a mapping from one to the other. The usual assumption is that the projections producing those keys and values are fixed after training. They're learned during pretraining, then frozen, and only the memory state changes at test time. So the model can change *what it stores*, but not *how it represents* the things it's storing.

That becomes a real limitation once you care about adaptability. The value projection decides what information from the current token is worth writing into memory and in what form. If that projection is static, the model is committed to one notion of "what's important," fixed when training ended. But the right thing to remember depends on context. In a long document, a codebase, or a conversation that shifts topic, the features that matter early may be quite different from the ones that matter later.

So when we let the value projection itself adapt in context, we're letting the model learn on the fly not only the associations but the representation of what gets associated. You can think of it as a kind of self-modification. The memory isn't just a passive store being written to. It participates in deciding what its own targets should be. That's one of the ideas behind self-referential or self-modifying memory modules: the components that generate the learning signal are also learnable at test time.

A few practical consequences follow from that.

First, the memory gets more expressive for a given size, because it isn't spending capacity on features a fixed projection deemed important that turn out to be irrelevant here.

Second, it helps with distribution shift. If the input at inference differs from what the model saw in training, a frozen value projection can feed the memory a poorly suited target, and no amount of memory updating fully fixes that. Adapting the projection gives you another degree of freedom to correct for it.

Third, and this is the more conceptual point, it moves us toward a view where learning isn't split cleanly into "training" and "inference." In the brain there isn't a hard boundary where some parts are fixed forever and others are plastic. Different components update at different rates, at different levels. Updating the value projection is one step toward that multi-timescale, nested picture of learning, where the model keeps refining both its memories and the way it forms them.

So for me it isn't just an engineering trick. It's part of a broader argument that if we want models that continually learn and adapt, we have to let more of the system be learnable in context, not only the memory state.

r001.rationale: The response says the value projection generates values and can adapt in context, but it does not state that the module uses the same mechanism to generate values and update its memory.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure, let me try to give some intuition. When we think about an associative memory in the Titans or Miras framing, what the module is really doing is learning a mapping from keys to values at test time. The memory is a neural network, and when a new token comes in, we treat the key as the input and the value as the target, and we take a gradient step on the memory so it gets better at recalling that value given that key. That's the "learning to memorize" idea.

Now, in a lot of architectures, the key and value projections are fixed after pretraining. The memory itself adapts, but what it's being asked to store is frozen. And that's a subtle limitation. Because the value projection determines what information about a token we actually commit to memory. If that projection was learned on the pretraining distribution, then when you move to a new domain, a long document, a new task at inference time, the model can only store the kinds of features it was trained to find useful. It can adapt how it associates things, but not what it decides is worth associating.

So when we make the value projection itself updatable, we're letting the model change its notion of what matters in context. The memory isn't just remembering better, it's deciding, on the fly, what to remember. And in our experiments, that turned out to be surprisingly important for in-context learning and for generalization to longer sequences than the model saw in training. You're essentially closing a loop: the memory sees the data, the data tells it what representation it should be storing, and that feeds back into the memorization objective. Without that, you have a learner with a fixed curriculum. With it, you have a learner that also gets to rewrite the curriculum a bit as it goes.

There's also a nice connection to the idea of self-referential or self-modifying models, where the parameters that generate the learning signal are themselves learned at test time. The value projection is one of the cleanest places to start doing that, because it directly shapes the target of the inner optimization. It's a small change conceptually, but it moves you from a system that adapts its memory to a system that adapts how it learns.

r001.rationale: The response says the memory learns a key-to-value mapping and updates using the value as a target, but it does not clearly state that the module generates values using the same mechanism it uses to update its memory.

astra-6.text:
The value projection determines what you actually store in memory. If you update the associations but keep that projection fixed, you can adapt which inputs retrieve which values, but you’re still constrained by a representation of the values that was learned beforehand.

Updating the value projection lets the memory adapt what it stores as well as how it retrieves it. That matters when the context changes, because the features that were useful during training may not be the features you need now. So it gives the module another degree of adaptability: it can change the representation of the information it’s trying to remember, rather than only changing the associations between fixed representations.

r001.rationale: The response discusses updating the value projection and memory associations, but does not state that value generation uses the same mechanism as memory updates.

sol-6.1.text:
The value projection determines what the memory actually stores. You can think of the key as the address and the value as the content associated with that address. If you update the memory but keep the value projection fixed, you can change the associations, but you’re still constrained to represent new information through a representation learned during training.

Updating the value projection lets the model adapt the content representation itself. As the context changes, it can learn which features are useful to retain, rather than only learning where to put them. So you’re adapting both the association and what gets associated, which gives the memory more flexibility when it encounters a new task or distribution.

r001.rationale: The response explains what the value projection stores and how updating it aids adaptation, but does not state that value generation uses the same mechanism as memory updates.
